title: Users of accounts and their decisions
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the users of accounts, what each needs from the figures, and how ratio results feed decisions such as lending to or investing in the business.

blocks.heading: Who reads the accounts
blocks.text: Users of accounts are the people and organisations with an interest in a business's financial results. Owners want to know what their stake is earning; managers want the detail that steers day-to-day decisions; lenders want evidence that loans will be repaid; suppliers want to know whether credit is safe to give; employees want evidence their jobs and wages are secure; government wants the taxable profit and a view of the firm's health. Each user asks a different question, so the same accounts get read for different needs - a spice importer in Istanbul deciding whether to extend credit to a customer reads the liquidity lines first, while that customer's own manager reads the expense detail first.

blocks.heading: What each user weighs
blocks.text: The needs differ, and so do the ratios each user weighs. A lender, or a supplier asked for credit, is likely to weigh the liquidity ratios - the current ratio and above all the acid test - because they show whether short-term debts can be met on time. An owner, or an investor thinking of buying in, is likely to weigh profitability - profit margin and ROCE - because these show the return the business earns on its sales and on its long-term funds. A manager reads them all: the gross profit margin to watch buying and selling, the profit margin to watch overheads, the liquidity pair to watch the payment calendar. None of these users is misreading the accounts; they are answering different questions with the same figures.

blocks.heading: Why ratios rather than raw figures
blocks.text: Raw accounts are hard to compare: one year's revenue of N$450 000 means little on its own. Ratio analysis turns the raw figures into percentages and proportions that can be set against earlier years, against other businesses in the same trade, and against the threshold a user has decided on in advance - a bank may decline to lend below an acid test of 1, whatever the profit. The comparison, not the figure itself, is what makes a result usable for a decision.

blocks.heading: From ratio to lending decision
blocks.text: Condition: a bank reads an acid test of 0.7 in a loan application. Mechanism: the figure suggests the business would rely on selling inventory to keep up repayments, so the bank expects a higher risk of missed dates. Consequence: the bank is likely to refuse the loan, or to grant it only against security and at a higher interest rate, because the extra risk has to be paid for. The same chain runs the other way: an acid test comfortably above 1, alongside a healthy profit margin, is likely to move the same decision towards approval, because repayment then looks secure on the dates as well as over the years.

blocks.heading: One figure is not a verdict
blocks.text: A single ratio for a single year is a snapshot. It may reflect a one-off event, an accounting choice or an unusual season, so users usually weigh several ratios, the trend over several years, and what they know of the business's context before deciding. An investor comparing two firms should also ask what each return depends on: a ROCE of 18% built on steady local demand may be worth more than 22% won from a passing fashion. Two users can read the same results and still decide differently, because their needs - and their tolerance of risk - differ, and that is a strength of the method rather than a flaw in it.
